title: How Skateboarding Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss skateboarding's history and mechanics. They cover the personal skating backgrounds of the hosts, the 1950s roller derby skateboard craze and its decline over safety concerns, the 1970s clay wheels and the urethane wheel that changed skating, the trucks and kicktail, the Zephyr Crew and the Del Mar contest, the Dogtown-era drained-pool skating and Tony Alva's first vert air, the Powell Peralta Bones Brigade and 1980s revival with videos, the early 1990s slump and X Games-driven return, and the deck's construction, grip tape, and graphics. They then explain stance (regular and goofy foot), skating styles (downhill, freestyle, vert, street), skate parks, the ollie, and common trick terms. The episode closes with listener mail about Josh's past case of the bends.

segments.title: Opening banter and skateboarding memories
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the hot recording booth and the word facetious, then share their own childhood skateboarding experiences, including clay wheels, early boards, and failed kickflips.

segments.title: Early skateboard history and the 1950s-60s craze
segments.summary: The hosts describe the four waves of skateboarding and the origin of the skateboard from homemade scooters and roller skate wheels. The first commercial board, the Roller Derby skate, came out in 1959, and skateboarding boomed in the early 1960s before safety concerns caused it to fade by about 1965.

segments.title: Clay wheels, urethane wheels, and the Zephyr Crew
segments.summary: Clay wheels in the late 1960s and early 1970s improved on steel but still caused injuries. Frank Nasworthy's urethane wheel in 1972 gave a smooth, grippy ride, and trucks allowed turning. The Zephyr Crew's Del Mar contest then brought skating to wider attention.

segments.title: Drought pool skating and the rise of vert
segments.summary: During a mid-1970s California drought, skaters drained backyard pools and skated them. Tony Alva, among others, pushed the pool skating forward, and he eventually caught air over the coping, which led to vert skating. Alva then founded his own company at about age nineteen.

segments.title: Sponsored pro teams, the Bones Brigade, and the 1980s revival
segments.summary: Zephyr alumni formed sponsored teams whose pros toured and did demos, spreading the sport. Skating declined in the late 1970s and became linked with punks. In the early 1980s the Powell Peralta Bones Brigade, including Tony Hawk, changed its image. Cheap VHS tapes of their videos helped spread skating, and the hosts discuss favorite riders.

segments.title: Early 1990s slump and return through the X Games
segments.summary: Skating slumped in the early 1990s, reportedly due to the recession. The X Games and Tony Hawk's video games brought the fourth wave back. The hosts note the 1980s nostalgia that revived old decks and shoes.

segments.title: Anatomy of the skateboard: deck, trucks, wheels, grip tape
segments.summary: The three main parts are the deck, trucks, and wheels. Trucks can be loose or tight, and wheels use polyurethane with bearings. The deck is laminated wood veneer pressed in a hydraulic mold, sealed, and given graphics and grip tape. Grip tape was invented for scooters by Ferdinand Schmidt, and the hosts discuss 1980s graphics.

segments.title: Riding stance: regular foot and goofy foot
segments.summary: The hosts explain regular foot and goofy foot stances, noting that mongo foot is pushing from the front. Stance usually follows handedness. They describe a way to find your stance by seeing which foot you step back with when someone pushes you.

segments.title: Skating styles: downhill, freestyle, vert, street, and skate parks
segments.summary: The hosts describe downhill slalom and its dangers, freestyle tricks on flat ground, vert skating in pools and ramps, and street skating on obstacles. They discuss 1970s skate park closures over liability and later reopening, skate park design complaints, and the Venice Beach bowl.

segments.title: The ollie and trick terminology
segments.summary: The ollie, invented by Alan Gelfand in the 1970s, is explained as a way to jump with the board attached to your feet. The hosts cover the world record ollie and define front side, backside, one eighty, 900 and 1080 spins, fakey, pop shove-it, grinds, slides, kickflip, and manual.

segments.title: Safety gear and getting started
segments.summary: The hosts recommend helmets, knee pads, and elbow pads, and mention local ordinances requiring them at skate parks. Wrist guards are discussed as a common injury source. They suggest starting with the HowStuffWorks search and buying a board.

segments.title: Listener mail: Josh and the bends
segments.summary: Listener Ben points out that Josh denied ever having the bends in a Diving Bell episode even though he had described a mild case during a scuba dive episode. Josh admits a mild case of the bends after surfacing too fast and says he had forgotten it.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: The hosts give social media and email contact details and point to the website for more information.
